newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh's massive cyclone haunts survivors.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh's massive cyclone haunts survivors.

text.p: Staring blankly at the restless sea almost two days after a cyclone battered Bangladesh's vast flat coastline, survivor Abdus Shukur said the horrific winds would haunt him forever.
"Those horrific hours I will never forget. It looked as though the whole island would be blown away," the 32-year-old fisherman said on Wednesday on Maheshkhali island.
"At one time, I thought it would never stop," Shukur said of what he called an unforgettable experience.
Hundreds and thousands of Bangladeshi islanders like Shakur, though familiar with storms at sea, were bewildered by the prolonged onslaught of Monday's 200 kph (124 mph) cyclone.
They said it was different from other cyclones because it lasted so long.
"I have seen many cyclones in my life, but not such a prolonged one," said Jogendra Lal Das, 60, from nearby Kutubdia island.
Islanders said the 1991 cyclone, the country's worst that killed at least 138,000 people, had lasted only four hours but the latest storm continued for more than 12 hours.

"It was unique in its very unpredictable behaviour. Sometimes we thought it had come to an end, but soon it regained strength and slammed back on us more fiercely. Also, it changed course frequently," Das said.
In Teknaf, the southernmost tip of Bangladesh, the cyclone lasted 15 hours with varying windspeeds, according to meteorology officials.
Many islanders said they had to remain in cyclone shelters much longer than on previous occasions.

"Never I experienced such a (suffocating) situation. Thousands of men, women and children remained huddled for 12 to 15 hours at a stretch in shelters without food and water," said one Maheshkhali student.
Officials in Kutubdia said two children died of suffocation in a cyclone shelter.
With the winds gaining strength in Kutubdia, islanders crowded the shelters shortly after daybreak on Monday and remained there until midnight.
Weather officials said casualties had been lower this time because the cyclone struck during the day and at low tide.
"It's Bhagwan (god) who saved us this time. If it had come during high tide, all of us would have washed away," said Das, a member of Bangladesh's minority Hindu community.
The confirmed death toll from Monday's cyclone was 112 so far, officials said. But some 1,500 fishermen were unaccounted for in the Bay of Bengal and the toll might rise.
Unofficial sources put the death toll at up to 500.
